name: LM2611AMFX_NOPB
title: 1.4 MHz Cuk converter with integrated switch, negative output
summary: The LM2611 is a 1.4 MHz fixed-frequency, current-mode PWM regulator with a built-in DMOS switch, made for Cuk converters that turn a positive supply (2.7 V to 14 V) into a regulated negative output. Inductors at both input and output keep ripple current low at both ports (about 1 mVp-p output ripple); the high frequency allows small inductors and ceramic capacitors. Two resistors on the NFB pin set the output against a −1.23 V reference; compensation and cycle-by-cycle current limiting are internal, and a shutdown pin drops supply current below 1 µA. Grade A (LM2611A) has a 1.2 A switch limit and 0.5 Ω switch; grade B 0.9 A and 0.7 Ω. Uses include MR head, CCD, LCD and GaAs FET bias.
key_figures: 1.2 A typ (grade A), 0.9 A typ (grade B)

pins.name: SW
pins.function: Drain of the internal power switch. Goes to the junction of the input inductor and the Cuk capacitor.

pins.name: GND
pins.function: Ground for both the analog circuitry and the power switch.

pins.name: NFB
pins.function: Negative feedback input. A resistor divider from the output to this pin sets the output voltage.

pins.name: SHDN
pins.function: Shutdown control, active low. Tied to VIN the part runs; pulled to ground it shuts down.

pins.name: VIN
pins.function: Supply for the analog circuitry and the power stage. A 0.1 µF ceramic capacitor close to the pin removes high-frequency noise.

notes: Stress beyond these ratings can permanently damage the part; they are stress limits only, and operation is specified only within the recommended operating conditions. Long exposure at these limits can degrade reliability.

circuits.title: 5 V to −5 V inverting Cuk converter (Figure 24)
circuits.description: A single 5 V rail feeds both the chip and the power stage and is inverted to −5 V at up to 300 mA. While the switch is on, L1 charges from the input and CCUK feeds L2; while it is off, L1 refills CCUK through the Schottky D. RFB1 and RFB2 from the output to NFB set the level against the −1.23 V reference, and CFF across RFB1 adds a zero-pole pair for transient response. SHDN is tied to VIN so the converter always runs. Changing RFB2 gives another output voltage.

circuits.title: 9 V to −5 V inverting Cuk converter (Figure 27)
circuits.description: The 5 V version moved to a 9 V input, with both inductors at 10 µH. The chip and the power stage share the 9 V rail; SHDN is tied to it. RFB1/RFB2 set −5 V, CFF across RFB1 shapes the loop, and D is the Cuk rectifier from the CCUK/L2 node to ground. Changing RFB2 gives another output voltage.

circuits.title: 12 V to −5 V inverting Cuk converter (Figure 29)
circuits.description: A 12 V input inverted to −5 V, with 22 µH inductors, a 2.2 µF coupling capacitor and a 1000 pF feed-forward capacitor. Chip supply and SHDN come from the 12 V rail. Changing RFB2 gives another output voltage.

circuits.title: Cuk converter from a 12 V power rail with a 5 V bias rail (Figure 21)
circuits.description: The power stage runs from 12 V while the chip's VIN and SHDN sit on a separate 5 V bias rail, giving −5 V at 375 mA. L1A and L1B are separate, uncoupled 22 µH inductors; CCUK carries energy from the input side to the output side; D is the rectifier from the CCUK/L1B node to ground. RFB1/RFB2 set the output against the reference and CFF across RFB1 improves the transient response. A capacitor decouples the 5 V rail at the chip.
notes: Inductors: Sumida CLS62-220 or Murata LZH3C220, uncoupled.

circuits.title: Separate power and bias supplies (Figure 31)
circuits.description: A 12 V supply provides the converted power and a low-current 5 V supply biases the chip (VIN and SHDN), with CBYP decoupling the bias rail. The bias rail must stay within 2.7 V to 14 V while the power rail may run from 0 V up to 36 V less the output magnitude, so a higher power rail gives more output current than one rail limited to 14 V. Output −5 V at 375 mA; RFB1/RFB2 set it and CFF shapes the loop.

circuits.title: Shutdown and soft-start (Figure 32)
circuits.description: The single-supply Cuk converter with a soft-start network on SHDN. RSS pulls SHDN up to VIN; CSS couples SHDN to the output. At start-up the part toggles between running and shutdown while the output falls slowly to its final value, spreading the start-up energy over a longer time and lowering the input current spikes; the part has no soft-start of its own. VSHDN is also brought out as a control point.
notes: L1A and L1B carry polarity dots.

circuits.title: High duty cycle and load current (Figure 35)
circuits.description: A −5 V Cuk converter for inputs from 2.7 V to 14 V that keeps working at duty cycles above 0.5 (input below the output magnitude) and at high load. The lower feedback leg is split into RFB2 (1 kΩ) in series with RFB3 (9 kΩ), and CFF2 (1 µF) across RFB3 adds a low-frequency lag pole-zero pair that keeps the loop stable in that corner; CFF1 across RFB1 is the usual feed-forward capacitor. SHDN is tied to VIN.

equations.name: Cuk output voltage
equations.note: From volt-second balance on either inductor; the output is inverted and its magnitude may be above or below VIN.

equations.name: Average input-inductor current
equations.expr: IL1 = D / (1 − D) × IL2 = D / (1 − D) × IOUT

equations.name: Input-inductor ripple
equations.note: Used with Equation 3 to size the inductor cores.

equations.name: Peak switch current
equations.expr: ISW(PEAK) = IL1 + IL2 + ΔiL1 + ΔiL2 = IOUT × (1 + D / (1 − D)) + (VIN × D × TS / 2) × (1/L1 + 1/L2)
equations.note: The switch carries the sum of both inductor currents. The peak must stay below the current limit (1.2 A typical) and is also bounded by the thermal resistance of the SOT-23 package, given with this equation as θJA = 265 °C/W.

equations.note: Because the pole depends on the divider ratio, it closes on the zero as the output nears −1.26 V.

operation.text: A fixed-frequency (1.4 MHz) current-mode PWM controller with its power switch, a low-RDS(ON) DMOS FET, and switch current sensing on chip. NFB drives an internal error amplifier through a type II/III compensation network that is entirely inside the part; a ramp generator adds slope compensation. The reference is −1.23 V, which suits a Cuk converter producing a negative output from a positive input. Grade A: 1.2 A limit, 0.5 Ω switch. Grade B: 0.9 A limit, 0.7 Ω switch.

With the switch closed and the diode off, the source charges L1 and the Cuk capacitor charges L2, which supplies the output. With the switch open, L1 recharges the Cuk capacitor through the diode and L2 delivers its energy to the load. Because there is an inductor in series with both the input and the output, the port currents on both sides are continuous and triangular with little ripple, unlike a buck-boost or flyback inverter. Each inductor sees VIN while the switch conducts; when it is open, VOUT does. The Cuk capacitor holds VIN − VOUT. The output can reach −(36 V − VIN(MAX)).

The internal compensation is designed for L1 and L2 between 10 µH and 22 µH. Pick values that hold peak-to-peak ripple below 0.3 A of the average current, then check the peak switch current against the current limit at maximum load over the input range; if it is too high, raise the inductance. Above 22 µH, stability needs checking across the operating range. Smaller inductance gives a smaller, cheaper design at the price of more ripple.

A dedicated comparator compares the switch current with a fixed limit reference, so the limit does not depend on other conditions. When the switch current passes the limit, the switch turns off for the rest of that period. The switch current is iL1 + iL2, so both inductor currents count toward the maximum load.

The input current is continuous, so the input capacitor sees small ripple, growing as L1 is made smaller. It must carry the RMS current of Equation 7. A good-quality capacitor of 10 µF or more avoids interaction with the source impedance, and a ceramic bypass of 0.1 µF or 1 µF goes on VIN (pin 5), within 0.2 inch of the pin.

The output capacitor must carry the RMS current of Equation 8, about 30 mA to 180 mA across inductors of 10 µH to 22 µH, outputs from −3.3 V to −10 V and inputs from 2.7 V to 30 V (30 V only with split supplies); the worst case is set by L1,2, VOUT(MAX) and VIN(MAX). Ceramic capacitors suit the part, keeping the ESR zero high; keep fESR above 80 kHz. Low-ESR tantalum parts usually handle 180 mA at 10 V or more, but their ESR can pull fESR low enough to make the loop unstable.

Compensation is internal, but a capacitor CFF across RFB1 adds a zero-pole pair that raises phase margin and bandwidth and so improves load-step response. The best zero position depends on D, IOUT, COUT, L1, L2 and CCUK; it usually lies between 5 kHz and 20 kHz. Because the pole moves toward the zero as the output nears −1.26 V, CFF does little when |VOUT| is under 3.3 V. Leaving a footprint for CFF and tuning it by load-step or loop-gain measurement is advised. The 5 V to −5 V circuit was measured with a 130 mA to 400 mA load step, with CFF = 1 nF and with CFF disconnected.
The reference magnitude is 1.23 V. Use 50 kΩ or less in the divider because of the NFB pin's bias current.

As the load falls, the energy carried by the Cuk capacitor eventually exceeds what the load needs and the surplus pushes the output out of regulation. The part detects this and changes to a pulse-skipping (hysteretic) mode, in which output ripple is slightly higher than the very low ripple of normal PWM operation.

Above 163 °C junction temperature the driver is disabled and the switch stays off until the junction cools to 155 °C, when switching resumes. Cooling from 163 °C to 155 °C takes about 10 ms with the switch off.
Pulling SHDN low stops the converter and cuts supply current to under 1 µA (0.024 µA typical). SHDN at VIN runs the part.

VIN of the chip can be biased from a low-current supply (2.7 V to 14 V) while L1 is fed from a separate power supply of 0 V to (36 − |VOUT|) V. A higher power supply raises the available output current beyond what one supply limited to the 14 V VIN rating would give.

There is no internal soft-start; without one, the inrush at start-up may reach a multiple of the steady load current. Coupling SHDN to the output through a capacitor toggles the part between run and shutdown while the output ramps, spreading the energy over a longer time and lowering the input current spikes. Start-up input current: 272 mA marked with the soft-start network, 405 mA without it.

The duty cycle climbs past 50% once the input falls below the output magnitude. At high duty cycle combined with high load, a lag pole-zero pair in the feedback network (RFB3 with CFF2) is needed for stability.

The supply must stay within the absolute maximum rating. Long input leads add inductance and resistance; with low-ESR ceramic input capacitors that inductance can form an under-damped resonance and cause overvoltage spikes at VIN when the supply is switched on or off.

Keep the L1-to-SW and CCUK-to-SW connections as short as possible. Place the feedback resistors next to NFB so the high-impedance node is small. Route the feedback trace from the output away from the two switching nodes (L1/CCUK and CCUK/L2/D) and away from under L1 and L2. Put a 0.1 µF bypass capacitor CBYP next to the VIN and GND pins.
ESD protection is limited; store the parts with the leads shorted or in conductive foam to protect the MOS gates.
